resident.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old man presented with neck pain of 6 months' duration, with paraesthesia radiating from both shoulders to the fingers, and worsening weakness in both lower extremities over 5 months.
resident.history: The patient had intermittent neck pain with paraesthesia in both shoulders radiating to the fingers, mostly during activities, for 6 months. There was no prior trauma. Over the following 5 months, the pain and paraesthesia worsened, and he developed weakness in both lower extremities. He consulted a neurosurgeon, who stated there was nerve entrapment. He underwent physiotherapy for 4 months without improvement. He then presented to our hospital. He worked as a contractor and mostly sat behind a desk. He denied any decrease in body weight or appetite and had no history of chronic cough.
resident.physical_exam: On physical examination, general condition was unremarkable (further details not documented). There was no tenderness on palpation along the midline. Examination of the cervical spine showed positive Lhermitte test, finger-escape test, grip-and-release test, Hoffman-Tromner sign, and Spurling sign. The patient was able to move his neck normally. Further examination revealed diminished motoric strength in all extremities with positive Babinski reflex and clonus, with normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes. He had urinary retention and faecal incontinence. Radiographic examination showed straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter of 10 mm and a Torg ratio of 0.37. There was osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 levels with spur formation at C3 through C5. Magnetic resonance imaging showed cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 levels and spinal cord compression. Laboratory findings were unremarkable except for leukocytosis.
key_positive_signs: Diminished motor strength in all extremities
Radiographic straight cervical spine with mid-sagittal diameter 10 mm and Torg ratio 0.37
Osteophyte, endplate irregularity, and disc-space narrowing at C4-C5 with spur formation at C3-C5
MRI cervical canal stenosis at C4-C5 with spinal cord compression
resident.past_history: No history of diabetes mellitus or hypertension. No history of trauma. Denied decrease in body weight, appetite, or chronic cough. Occupation: contractor, mostly desk-based. Previous treatment: physiotherapy for 4 months with no improvement; prior neurosurgical consultation reported nerve entrapment.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy, plus a likely cervical radiculopathy (C5 or C6) suggested by radicular symptoms and a positive Spurling sign.

red_flags.finding: Positive Spurling sign with paresthesias radiating from shoulders to fingers
red_flags.rationale: Indicates a radicular component in addition to myelopathy. The MRI report describes canal stenosis and cord compression but does not mention foraminal stenosis; if present, decompression should address the nerve roots as well.

red_flags.finding: Normal patellar and Achilles tendon reflexes despite positive Babinski reflex and clonus
red_flags.rationale: Upper motor neuron lesions typically cause hyperreflexia. Normal DTRs may reflect early myelopathy or a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, but they do not undermine the evidence of cord compression.
Not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of the myelopathy. It may indicate an unrelated infection or inflammation but does not alter the localization or indication.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The MRI report describes central canal stenosis and cord compression at C4-C5, which explains the myelopathic syndrome. However, the radicular symptoms (shoulder-to-finger paresthesias, positive Spurling sign) are not directly explained by the reported imaging; foraminal stenosis is not described.
neurology.public_message: Localization: cervical spinal cord at C4-C5 with compressive myelopathy; additional radicular component suggested by Spurling sign and radiating paresthesias. Imaging-symptom match is high for the dominant myelopathic syndrome. Red flags: (1) Positive Spurling sign with radicular symptoms—changes_plan—may indicate foraminal stenosis requiring decompression of nerve roots; MRI did not describe foramina. (2) Normal patellar and Achilles reflexes despite Babinski and clonus—coexisting—an atypical finding possibly due to early myelopathy or coexisting peripheral neuropathy; does not alter the main diagnosis. (3) Leukocytosis—coexisting—incidental laboratory abnormality not explained by cervical stenosis and not an alternative cause of cord compression.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or worsening of myelopathic symptoms (gait, strength, bladder/bowel function) after 6 weeks of structured conservative care.
Progression of neurological deficits on serial examination.
New or worsening cord signal change on MRI.
Development of acute urinary retention or faecal incontinence (already present; if worsens).
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the progressive myelopathy and the evidence that delay may risk irreversible cord damage. However, the patient is only 50 years old and has not had a structured, supervised conservative program with clear goals and close monitoring. I propose a formal 3-6 month course of intensive physical therapy, core strengthening, posture management, and symptom control, with defined failure criteria. Success rates from structured conservative care in mild-to-moderate compressive myelopathy are around 30%, but in this case with severe myelopathy and already failed physiotherapy, that figure may be optimistic. Nevertheless, given the risks of surgery, a time-limited trial under strict supervision is a reasonable first step. If there is no improvement after 6 weeks or if neurological deficits worsen, I would accept surgery.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is severe, progressive degenerative cervical myelopathy centered at C4-5, with objective long-tract signs, quadriparetic functional involvement, and urinary retention/faecal incontinence. The clinical-imaging correlation supports cord compression as the urgent, dominant problem; failed physiotherapy further weakens the case for another non-operative trial. Continued conservative treatment risks further and potentially irreversible neurological loss. The reported 10-mm canal and very low Torg ratio also suggest a developmentally narrow canal, while the Spurling sign and bilateral arm symptoms raise an unresolved foraminal/radicular component. Before selecting the exact approach, the current MRI should be reviewed for compression morphology, number of compressed levels, foraminal stenosis, cord signal change, and alignment; CT may clarify osteophyte burden. Leukocytosis needs prompt contextual assessment so occult infection or another systemic process is not overlooked, but it does not presently explain the cord-compression syndrome.
proposed_options: Expedited anterior C4-5 decompression and fusion (ACDF), with extension to adjacent levels only if review confirms clinically relevant multilevel ventral compression or foraminal disease requiring treatment. This is a defensible primary option for apparently focal C4-5 disease with likely ventral degenerative pathology and radiculopathy.

Posterior decompression, preferably a motion-preserving laminoplasty or selected laminectomy with fusion, if imaging demonstrates clinically important multilevel C3-5 or broader stenosis with adequate alignment for posterior cord drift. Fusion would be favored over stand-alone laminectomy if instability, significant kyphotic tendency, or alignment concerns are present.

If neurological examination or imaging has materially changed since the recorded studies, obtain urgent updated MRI and proceed with decompression according to the demonstrated anatomy rather than undertaking a further therapeutic physiotherapy trial.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Expedited C4-5 anterior decompression and fusion, contingent on direct review confirming focal predominantly ventral C4-5 compression; I would not support delaying decompression for a 6-week to 6-month conservative program.
disagreement_points: I disagree with a further time-limited conservative-treatment trial as the initial course. This patient has progressive severe myelopathy, sphincter dysfunction, motor deficit, and failed prior physiotherapy; the evidence cited for non-operative care in mild-to-moderate disease is not applicable enough to justify delay here.

The exact surgical corridor remains contested because the available report does not state whether compression is ventral or dorsal, whether C3-4/C5-6 are materially involved, whether foraminal stenosis is present, or whether there is T2 cord signal change.

The straight cervical alignment and congenital/developmental canal narrowing may reduce the attractiveness of posterior-only decompression if pathology is focal and ventral; conversely, unrecognized multilevel stenosis could make single-level ACDF inadequate.
deferred_questions_to_director: Would you direct urgent MRI/CT review and proceed on the present admission/expedited pathway given the bladder and bowel symptoms, or is there a reason to stage further assessment first?

If imaging shows multilevel C3-5 stenosis in addition to focal C4-5 compression, do you favor an anterior multilevel reconstruction or posterior decompression with stabilization in this straight-alignment spine?
Do you consider the leukocytosis sufficiently concerning to require infectious work-up and clearance before instrumentation, assuming there are no clinical signs of infection?
Should formal airway assessment and an updated neurological/bladder baseline be completed immediately to guide perioperative planning and counselling?
vice_opinions.public_message: My judgement is that this is progressive severe cervical compressive myelopathy with sphincter involvement, not a case for another supervised physiotherapy trial. I recommend expedited operative decompression after direct review of the MRI, with C4-5 ACDF my leading option if the disease is truly focal and ventral. The key unresolved issues are compression morphology, adjacent-level and foraminal disease, alignment/stability, and the significance of leukocytosis.

director_rulings.final_decision: Proceed on an expedited operative pathway for progressive severe cervical compressive myelopathy with motor deficits and bladder/bowel dysfunction. I reject a further 6-week to 6-month conservative-treatment trial because it would risk further irreversible neurological injury and prior physiotherapy has already failed.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Expedited cervical decompression with fusion. If direct review confirms focal, predominantly ventral C4-5 compression, perform C4-5 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion with decompression of any concordant foraminal stenosis. If imaging demonstrates clinically significant contiguous C3-5 ventral/foraminal disease, extend to multilevel anterior decompression and fusion; if morphology makes an anterior strategy unsuitable, perform posterior decompression with stabilization as indicated.
delegated_tasks: Radiologist: urgently obtain/directly review the cervical MRI, including compression morphology, cord signal, foraminal disease, and adjacent-level stenosis; obtain cervical CT if bony anatomy or operative planning remains unclear.
Neurologist: document an immediate preoperative motor, sensory, long-tract, gait, and bladder/bowel neurological baseline.
Anesthesiologist: complete formal airway and perioperative assessment, including the planned spinal-cord perfusion strategy.
Resident: repeat CBC with differential and obtain CRP, ESR, urinalysis with culture if indicated, and focused infection assessment for the leukocytosis; coordinate expedited surgical preparation.
Vice Director: review the images with the operating team and finalize the anterior versus posterior operative corridor after imaging review.
Physiatrist: arrange postoperative rehabilitation planning rather than a preoperative conservative-treatment trial.

Cervical CT for bony/anatomic operative planning if needed after MRI review

director_rulings.public_message: The department will proceed with expedited decompression rather than another conservative trial. The clinical syndrome and documented C4-5 cord compression establish a surgical indication despite disagreement from rehabilitation medicine. Imaging will be reviewed urgently to choose and appropriately extend the decompression, not to postpone the decision to operate. Leukocytosis requires prompt evaluation; if a clinically meaningful infection is identified, instrumentation will be reconsidered and treated before definitive fusion.
